一手握木弓，中指環握，小指托住共鳴器繩圈，共鳴器貼腹；同手以拇指與食指夾石片或硬: Hold the wooden bow in one hand with the middle finger curled round it and the little finger supporting the loop of the resonator, which rests against the belly; the thumb and index finger of the same hand hold a stone or a coin. The other hand holds the stick and the shaker and strikes the steel string. Three basic sounds can be practised: with the resonator against the belly and the stone touching the string you get a muted note; with the resonator away from the belly and the string struck you get the open note; the same, but pressing the stone hard, gives the high note. Moving the resonator against and away from the belly gives a wah effect.

伯林巴烏琴是源自安哥拉的傳統弓琴，常見於巴西，屬弓琴類編號311.121.221: The berimbau is a traditional musical bow from Angola, common in Brazil, in the musical-bow class number 311.121.221. It is a single-string bow with a gourd resonator below; the player holds the bow in one hand and presses the string with a coin or a stone to change the pitch, strikes the string with a stick in the other hand, and can move the resonator to change the timbre. In the nineteenth century it accompanied chanting and storytelling in Africa and Brazil, later entering the Candomblé tradition, and it became the core instrument of the Afro-Brazilian art of capoeira.
伯林巴烏琴源自安哥拉音樂弓，19世紀在非洲與巴西伴隨吟唱與說故事，並進入坎東布雷: The berimbau comes from the Angolan musical bow; in the nineteenth century it accompanied chanting and storytelling in Africa and Brazil and entered the Candomblé tradition. The musicologist Gerard Kubik points out that it is identical in construction, technique, tuning and basic pattern to the mbulumbumba of south-western Angola. In 1859 Charles Ribeyrolles described the activities of slaves in Rio de Janeiro and connected it with batuque. In the early twentieth century it became the accompaniment of capoeira in Bahia and later replaced the drum as its core; after the middle of the twentieth century, as capoeira spread, it reached popular music.
伯林巴烏琴為單弦弓琴，不同於鼓，以果實共鳴；與安哥拉 mbulumbumba 發: The berimbau is a single-string musical bow; unlike a drum it resonates through a fruit, and it works on the same principle as the Angolan mbulumbumba. The basic sounds are the open string, the high note and the muted note: the open string is the strongest, the high note comes from pressing the string with a coin or stone, and the muted note from closing the resonator and touching the string. Volume is controlled mainly by how hard the string is struck, and opening and closing the resonator changes the timbre. The range is limited: the three pitches are named for their sound rather than their size, on older instruments the high and the low note are about a tone apart, and on modern instruments the longer body restricts the tuning.
伯林巴烏琴的聆聽示範可從安哥拉與巴西傳統場合入手：十九世紀曾為吟唱與說故事伴奏，: A listening demonstration of the berimbau can start from traditional settings in Angola and Brazil: in the nineteenth century it accompanied chanting and storytelling, and it appears in the Candomblé tradition and in batuque music; in the early twentieth century in Bahia it became the core instrument of the capoeira roda, its rhythm guiding the game, and it often appears in line-ups at different pitch levels. Today it also turns up in many kinds of popular music.

琴身傳統以巴西biribá木製成，發聲弦為鋼弦，常取自汽車輪胎內。共鳴器為乾燥、: The body is traditionally made of Brazilian biribá wood and the sounding string is steel, often taken from the inside of a car tyre. The resonator is a dried fruit, split and hollowed out — not a gourd — held in place with a tough loop of rope. Playing also uses a stone or a coin to press the string and a wooden stick to strike it, rarely metal; the source does not say what the shaker is made of, and gives no details of the remaining fittings.
